pairs.source_text: Talis ab armiferis Priameius hospes Amyclis Candida cum rapta coniuge vela dedit;
pairs.question: Unde Priameius hospes Paris cum rapta coniuge vela dedit?
pairs.question_en: From where did Paris, Priam's son and guest, set sail with his stolen wife?
pairs.derivation: Paris ('Priameius hospes', the guest who betrayed his host) sailing from Laconian Amyclae with Helen. Place-fact of the canonical abduction; 'ab... Amyclis... rapta coniuge vela dedit' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Talis erat qui te curru victore ferebat, Vecta peregrinis Hippodamia rotis.
pairs.question: Quis heros Hippodamiam curru victore avexit?
pairs.question_en: Which hero carried off Hippodamia on his victorious chariot?
pairs.derivation: The chariot-race of Pelops for Hippodamia ('curru victore... vecta peregrinis rotis'): the winner is unnamed in the couplet but is by canon Pelops, the 'foreign wheels' marking the stranger-suitor. Canonical bridal myth.

pairs.source_text: Nunc mihi, siquando, puer et Cytherea, favete, Nunc Erato, nam tu nomen amoris habes.
pairs.question: Quae Musa nomen amoris habet, ut Ovidius eam invocans ait?
pairs.question_en: Which Muse bears the name of love, as Ovid says in invoking her?
pairs.derivation: Erato, the Muse whose name contains Eros/amor, invoked for love-poetry ('nam tu nomen amoris habes'). Shared literary-mythological knowledge; name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Daedalus ut clausit conceptum crimine matris Semibovemque virum semivirumque bovem,
pairs.question: Quod monstrum, crimine matris conceptum, Daedalus inclusit?
pairs.question_en: What monster, conceived by its mother's crime, did Daedalus shut in?
pairs.answer_en: The Minotaur, half-bull man and half-man bull.
pairs.derivation: Daedalus builder of the Minotaur's enclosure (the labyrinth); the proverb-famous line 'semibovemque virum semivirumque bovem' defines the monster of Pasiphae's crime. Canonical; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Remigium volucrum disponit in ordine pinnas, Et leve per lini vincula nectit opus, Imaque pars ceris adstringitur igne solutis, Finitusque novae iam labor artis erat.
pairs.question: Quibus rebus Daedalus pinnas alarum inter se ligavit?
pairs.question_en: With what did Daedalus bind the feathers of his wings together?
pairs.derivation: The construction of the wings: feathers set in order like oarage, tied with linen threads, the base bound with melted wax. Both materials verbatim; canonical Daedalus fact (the wax carries the story).

pairs.source_text: Nam sive aetherias vicino sole per auras Ibimus, impatiens cera caloris erit: Sive humiles propiore freto iactabimus alas, Mobilis aequoreis pinna madescet aquis. Inter utrumque vola; ventos quoque, nate, timeto,
pairs.question: Qua via Daedalus filio Icaro volandum esse praecepit?
pairs.question_en: By what course did Daedalus instruct his son Icarus to fly?
pairs.answer_en: Midway between the sun and the sea.
pairs.derivation: The famous middle-course instruction: too near the sun the wax melts, too near the sea the feathers soak — 'inter utrumque vola'. Canonical story-fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cum puer, incautis nimium temerarius annis, Altius egit iter, deseruitque patrem. Vincla labant, et cera deo propiore liquescit, Nec tenues ventos brachia mota tenent.
pairs.question: Qua de causa alae Icari in aere solutae sunt?
pairs.answer: Quod altius volavit et sole propiore cera liquefacta est.
pairs.question_en: Why did the wings of Icarus come apart in the air?
pairs.answer_en: Because he flew too high and the wax melted as the sun came nearer.
pairs.derivation: The fatal fall: Icarus left his father's course, flew too high, and the wax melted ('altius egit iter... cera deo propiore liquescit'). Canonical cause-fact with one checkable answer, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Decidit, atque cadens 'pater, o pater, auferor!' inquit, Clauserunt virides ora loquentis aquae. At pater infelix, nec iam pater, 'Icare!' clamat, 'Icare,' clamat 'ubi es, quoque sub axe volas?' 'Icare' clamabat, pinnas aspexit in undis. Ossa tegit tellus: aequora nomen habent.
pairs.question: Unde mare Icarium nomen traxit?
pairs.answer: Ab Icaro, qui in id decidit.
pairs.question_en: From whom did the Icarian Sea take its name?
pairs.answer_en: From Icarus, who fell into it.
pairs.derivation: The aition Ovid states: the boy fell, the land holds his bones, 'the waters hold his name' — the Icarian Sea. Name-fact of shared geography-myth; the Metamorphoses 8 version is not yet mined, so taken here.

pairs.source_text: Phasias Aesoniden, Circe tenuisset Ulixem, Si modo servari carmine posset amor.
pairs.question: Cuius filius erat Iason, qui 'Aesonides' dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Whose son was Jason, who is called 'Aesonides'?
pairs.derivation: Patronymic fact: Jason son of Aeson, here the beloved whom the 'Phasian woman' (Medea, of the river Phasis) could not hold by spells. Canonical; the patronymic is verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Non facient, ut vivat amor, Medeides herbae Mixtaque cum magicis nenia Marsa sonis.
pairs.question: Quae gens Italiae neniis magicis nota erat, ut apud Ovidium legitur?
pairs.question_en: Which Italian people was known for magical incantations, as one reads in Ovid?
pairs.derivation: The Marsi, proverbial in Italy for spells and snake-charming ('nenia Marsa'). Ethnographic fact of shared Roman lore; verbatim epithet.

pairs.source_text: Fallitur, Haemonias siquis decurrit ad artes, Datque quod a teneri fronte revellit equi.
pairs.question: Quae terra Graeciae artibus magicis ita nota erat, ut 'Haemoniae artes' pro veneficiis dicerentur?
pairs.question_en: Which land of Greece was so famous for magic arts that 'Haemonian arts' meant witchcraft?
pairs.derivation: Thessaly as the proverbial home of witches — 'Haemonias... artes' for love-magic. Ambient Roman lore (cf. Lucan, Apuleius); Haemonia = Thessaly is the standard identification.

pairs.source_text: Fallitur, Haemonias siquis decurrit ad artes, Datque quod a teneri fronte revellit equi.
pairs.question: Ex qua parte equi tenelli amatorium illud famosum revelli credebatur?
pairs.question_en: From what part of a young horse was the famous love-charm believed to be torn?
pairs.derivation: The hippomanes, the growth plucked from a foal's forehead and used in love-magic (cf. Vergil, Aen. 4.515) — Ovid names the practice while dismissing it. The belief, not the advice, is the fact; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sis licet antiquo Nireus adamatus Homero, Naiadumque tener crimine raptus Hylas,
pairs.question: A quibus raptus est tener Hylas?
pairs.question_en: By whom was the tender Hylas carried off?
pairs.derivation: Hylas, Hercules' young companion, snatched by the water-nymphs ('Naiadum... crimine raptus') — canonical Argonautic story. Verbatim; single answer.

pairs.source_text: Sis licet antiquo Nireus adamatus Homero, Naiadumque tener crimine raptus Hylas,
pairs.question: A quo poeta antiquo Nireus adamatus est, ut ait Ovidius?
pairs.question_en: By which ancient poet was Nireus 'beloved', as Ovid puts it?
pairs.derivation: Nireus, the beauty of the Greek host, 'loved' (celebrated) by old Homer (Iliad 2) — the shared literary fact that Nireus' fame for beauty rests on Homer. Verbatim, attributed.

pairs.source_text: Non formosus erat, sed erat facundus Ulixes, Et tamen aequoreas torsit amore deas.
pairs.question: Qua dote Ulixes, quamquam non formosus, deas aequoreas amore torsit?
pairs.question_en: By what gift did Ulysses, though not handsome, torment the sea-goddesses with love?
pairs.derivation: The canonical characterization: Ulysses 'non formosus sed facundus', whose speech won Calypso and Circe. Trait-fact verbatim; anchored to Ulysses.

pairs.source_text: Ille levi virga (virgam nam forte tenebat) Quod rogat, in spisso litore pingit opus. 'Haec' inquit 'Troia est' (muros in litore fecit): 'Hic tibi sit Simois; haec mea castra puta.
pairs.question: Cui deae Ulixes Troiam Simoentaque virga in litore depinxit?
pairs.question_en: For which goddess did Ulysses draw Troy and the Simois with a staff on the beach?
pairs.derivation: The Calypso inset: she begs the tale of Troy again and again, and Ulysses sketches Troy, the Simois, and the camps in the sand ('in spisso litore pingit'). Calypso is named just above ('illic quoque pulchra Calypso exigit Odrysii fata cruenta ducis'); both entities canonical.

pairs.source_text: Campus erat' (campumque facit), 'quem caede Dolonis Sparsimus, Haemonios dum vigil optat equos.
pairs.question: Quos equos Dolon, nocturnus explorator, praemium sibi optabat?
pairs.question_en: What horses did Dolon, the night spy, desire as his reward?
pairs.derivation: The Doloneia (Iliad 10): the Trojan spy Dolon slain by Ulysses and Diomedes, having bargained for Achilles' (Thessalian, 'Haemonian') horses. Verbatim; anchored to Dolon.

pairs.source_text: Illic Sithonii fuerant tentoria Rhesi: Hac ego sum captis nocte revectus equis.'
pairs.question: Cuius regis Thracii equos Ulixes nocte captos revexit?
pairs.question_en: Which Thracian king's horses did Ulysses carry off by night?
pairs.derivation: The night-raid on the camp of 'Sithonian' (Thracian) Rhesus and the capture of his horses — canonical Iliad 10 story told in Ulysses' own words. Verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Hoc decet uxores; dos est uxoria lites: Audiat optatos semper amica sonos.
pairs.question: Quae dos uxoria esse dicitur ioco proverbiali apud Ovidium?
pairs.question_en: What is said, in Ovid's proverbial joke, to be a wife's dowry?
pairs.derivation: 'Dos est uxoria lites' — the quotable quip that bickering is the dowry a wife brings. Proverb with a checkable point, verbatim and attributed.

pairs.source_text: Quid fuit asperius Nonacrina Atalanta? Succubuit meritis trux tamen illa viri. Saepe suos casus nec mitia facta puellae Flesse sub arboribus Milaniona ferunt;
pairs.question: Cuius viri meritis Atalanta Nonacrina tandem succubuit?
pairs.question_en: To which man's devoted services did Atalanta of Nonacris at last yield?
pairs.derivation: The Arcadian Atalanta ('Nonacrina') won by the long service of Milanion — canonical myth in its Arcadian version. Both names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sensit et Hylaei contentum saucius arcum: Sed tamen hoc arcu notior alter erat.
pairs.question: Cuius arcu Milanion, Atalantae amator, saucius est?
pairs.question_en: By whose bow was Milanion, Atalanta's lover, wounded?
pairs.derivation: The centaur Hylaeus, who assaulted Atalanta and wounded Milanion — mythographic fact stated verbatim ('Hylaei contentum saucius arcum'); 'the other, better-known bow' is Cupid's.

pairs.source_text: Seu iacies talos, victam ne poena sequatur, Damnosi facito stent tibi saepe canes:
pairs.question: Quis iactus in ludo talorum damnosus habebatur?
pairs.question_en: Which throw in the game of knucklebones was held ruinous?
pairs.derivation: In the tali game the throw called 'canes' (all aces) was the losing, money-costing cast — 'damnosi... canes'. Gaming realia every Roman knew (cf. Suetonius on Augustus' dicing); verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sive latrocinii sub imagine calculus ibit, Fac pereat vitreo miles ab hoste tuus.
pairs.question: Sub cuius rei imagine calculi in ludo latrunculorum ibant?
pairs.question_en: In the likeness of what did the pieces move in the game of latrunculi?
pairs.derivation: The board game latrunculi: pieces ('calculi', the 'miles', often of glass — 'vitreo... ab hoste') moving 'sub latrocinii imagine', in the image of a raid. Leisure-culture realia; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sive latrocinii sub imagine calculus ibit, Fac pereat vitreo miles ab hoste tuus.
pairs.question: E qua materia calculi ludi latrunculorum fieri solebant, ut Ovidius significat?
pairs.question_en: Of what material were the pieces of the latrunculi game commonly made, as Ovid indicates?
pairs.derivation: The 'glass enemy' ('vitreo... ab hoste') attests the standard glass gaming-pieces of latrunculi — material realia of Roman play, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ipse tene distenta suis umbracula virgis, Ipse fac in turba, qua venit illa, locum.
pairs.question: Quo instrumento, virgis distento, sol a dominis Romanis ambulantibus arcebatur?
pairs.question_en: With what implement, stretched on its ribs, was the sun kept off Roman ladies as they walked?
pairs.derivation: The umbraculum, the rib-stretched parasol carried over a lady — daily-life object named verbatim ('distenta suis umbracula virgis'); the holding-it advice is dropped, the object kept.

pairs.source_text: Ille, fatigata praebendo monstra noverca Qui meruit caelum, quod prior ipse tulit, Inter Ioniacas calathum tenuisse puellas Creditur, et lanas excoluisse rudes. Paruit imperio dominae Tirynthius heros:
pairs.question: Quis heros Tirynthius inter puellas Ionicas calathum tenuisse lanasque fecisse creditur?
pairs.question_en: Which Tirynthian hero is believed to have held the wool-basket among Ionian girls and worked wool?
pairs.derivation: Hercules in servitude to Omphale, spinning wool with the wool-basket — canonical story; 'Tirynthius heros' and 'qui meruit caelum' fix the referent as Hercules. 'Creditur' keeps the story-frame.

pairs.source_text: Ille, fatigata praebendo monstra noverca Qui meruit caelum, quod prior ipse tulit,
pairs.question: Quae dea, Herculis noverca, monstra ei praebendo fatigata est?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess, Hercules' stepmother, wearied herself supplying monsters against him?
pairs.derivation: Juno as the noverca who set the labors' monsters on Hercules until she was worn out ('fatigata praebendo monstra noverca') — canonical relationship-fact; the stepmother of Hercules is by canon Juno.

pairs.source_text: Cynthius Admeti vaccas pavisse Pheraei Fertur, et in parva delituisse casa.
pairs.question: Cuius regis vaccas Apollo Cynthius pavisse fertur?
pairs.question_en: Whose cattle is Cynthian Apollo said to have pastured?
pairs.derivation: Apollo the herdsman of Admetus of Pherae — canonical myth of the god's servitude; both names verbatim, 'fertur' keeping the tradition-frame.

pairs.source_text: Saepe tua poteras, Leandre, carere puella: Transnabas, animum nosset ut illa tuum.
pairs.question: Quo modo Leander ad puellam suam trans fretum ire solebat?
pairs.question_en: How did Leander cross the strait to reach his girl?
pairs.derivation: Leander swimming the Hellespont to Hero — canonical love-legend; 'transnabas' verbatim, anchored to the named Leander.

pairs.source_text: Porrige et ancillae, qua poenas luce pependit Lusa maritali Gallica veste manus.
pairs.question: Qua fraude Gallica manus poenas pependit die quo ancillae Romae festum agunt?
pairs.answer: Veste maritali lusa est (ancillis matronarum habitu indutis).
pairs.question_en: By what trick did the Gallic force pay the penalty, on the day the serving-maids keep festival at Rome?
pairs.answer_en: It was fooled by married women's dress (slave-girls dressed as matrons).
pairs.derivation: The ancillarum feriae (the Caprotine Nones, 7 July, outside the Fasti's Jan-June range): the enemy 'Gallic band' deceived when serving-maids went out dressed as brides/matrons. The aition-fact is verbatim ('lusa maritali Gallica veste manus').

pairs.source_text: Rure suburbano poteris tibi dicere missa, Illa vel in Sacra sint licet empta via.
pairs.question: In qua via Romae dona rustica emi poterant, quae e rure suburbano missa esse fingeres?
pairs.question_en: On what street in Rome could one buy 'country' gifts and pass them off as sent from a suburban farm?
pairs.derivation: The Sacra Via as a market street where produce and fancy goods were sold — Roman shopping topography ('vel in Sacra... empta via'); the deception-advice dropped, the venue-fact kept.

pairs.source_text: Adferat aut uvas, aut quas Amaryllis amabat++ At nunc castaneas non amat illa nuces.
pairs.question: Quas nuces Amaryllis pastoralis amabat, ut ex Vergilio notum Ovidius refert?
pairs.question_en: What nuts did the shepherdess Amaryllis love, as Ovid recalls from the famous Vergilian line?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's joke presupposes the celebrated Eclogue 2 line 'castaneasque nuces, mea quas Amaryllis amabat' — a literary tag every Roman reader carried. The checkable point (Amaryllis' chestnuts) is verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ipse licet venias Musis comitatus, Homere, Si nihil attuleris, ibis, Homere, foras.
pairs.question: Quid Homero ipsi, Musis comitato, eventurum esse ait Ovidius, si nihil attulerit?
pairs.question_en: What does Ovid say would happen to Homer himself, though escorted by the Muses, if he brought no gift?
pairs.answer_en: He would be shown the door.
pairs.derivation: Proverb-famous couplet on greedy times: even Homer goes out the door empty-handed. Quotable point, verbatim, attributed to Ovid.

pairs.locus: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 2.329-330 (lustratio sulpure et ovis)
pairs.source_text: Et veniat, quae lustret anus lectumque locumque, Praeferat et tremula sulpur et ova manu.
pairs.question: Quibus rebus anus Romana lectum locumque aegrotae lustrare solebat?
pairs.question_en: With what things did a Roman old woman customarily purify a sick person's bed and room?
pairs.derivation: Domestic purification rite: the crone lustrating the sickbed carrying sulphur and eggs — folk-religion realia stated verbatim; the courting-context dropped.

pairs.source_text: Coniugis admissum violataque iura marita est Barbara per natos Phasias ulta suos.
pairs.question: Quo modo Phasias Medea violata iura marita ulta est?
pairs.question_en: How did the Phasian woman, Medea, avenge her violated marriage rights?
pairs.answer_en: Through her own children (whom she slew).
pairs.derivation: Medea ('barbara Phasias', woman of the Phasis) avenging Jason's new marriage through their sons — the canonical infanticide, here stated verbatim ('per natos... ulta suos'); completes the Creusa pair from book I.

pairs.source_text: Altera dira parens haec est, quam cernis, hirundo: Aspice, signatum sanguine pectus habet.
pairs.question: Quae dira parens, quae natum occiderat, in hirundinem versa esse dicitur, sanguine pectus signata?
pairs.question_en: Which dread mother, who had killed her son, is said to have been turned into the swallow, her breast marked with blood?
pairs.derivation: The Procne-Itys myth: the child-slaying mother became the swallow whose red-marked breast records the blood. Ovid gives the periphrasis 'altera dira parens... hirundo'; the identification is canonical (Met. 6 not yet mined).

pairs.source_text: Audierat laurumque manu vittasque ferentem Pro nata Chrysen non valuisse sua:
pairs.question: Quibus insignibus ornatus Chryses sacerdos filiam suam frustra repetivit?
pairs.question_en: Bearing what emblems did the priest Chryses vainly seek back his daughter?
pairs.derivation: The opening of the Iliad as shared story: Chryses with the god's laurel and fillets refused by Agamemnon. 'Laurumque manu vittasque ferentem... Chrysen non valuisse' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Audierat, Lyrnesi, tuos, abducta, dolores, Bellaque per turpis longius isse moras.
pairs.question: Ex qua urbe Briseis, Achilli ablata, abducta erat?
pairs.question_en: From what city had Briseis, taken from Achilles, been carried off?
pairs.derivation: Briseis the 'Lyrnesian' captive ('Lyrnesi... abducta'), whose loss stalled the war — the epithet-fact of her origin at Lyrnesus, canonical from the Iliad. Verbatim; Briseis is the standard referent.

pairs.source_text: Haec tamen audierat: Priameida viderat ipsa: Victor erat praedae praeda pudenda suae.
pairs.question: Quam Priami filiam Agamemnon victor praedam domum advexit?
pairs.question_en: Which daughter of Priam did the victorious Agamemnon bring home as his prize?
pairs.derivation: The 'Priameis' seen by Clytemnestra with her own eyes is Cassandra, Agamemnon's captive — canonical identification of the periphrasis; 'victor... praedae praeda' verbatim for the relationship.

pairs.source_text: Inde Thyestiaden animo thalamoque recepit, Et male peccantem Tyndaris ulta virum.
pairs.question: Quem Tyndaris Clytaemnestra animo thalamoque recepit, virum peccantem ulta?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Clytemnestra, Tyndareus' daughter, take into her heart and bed to avenge her erring husband?
pairs.derivation: The 'Thyestiades' (son of Thyestes) taken by the 'Tyndaris' (Clytemnestra) — both canonical patronymic identifications; the adultery-as-revenge fact is verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sunt, qui praecipiant herbas, satureia, nocentes Sumere; iudiciis ista venena meis;
pairs.question: Quae herba inter amatoria sumenda praecipiebatur, quam Ovidius venenis adnumerat?
pairs.question_en: Which herb was prescribed to be taken as an aphrodisiac, though Ovid counts it among poisons?
pairs.derivation: Satureia (savory) as the reputed aphrodisiac herb of Roman lore — the belief is the fact (Ovid's disapproval is the frame). Named verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Candidus, Alcathoi qui mittitur urbe Pelasga, Bulbus et, ex horto quae venit, herba salax Ovaque sumantur, sumantur Hymettia mella,
pairs.question: Ex qua urbe Pelasga bulbi candidi mittebantur, ut Ovidius refert?
pairs.question_en: From what Pelasgian city were the white bulbs exported, as Ovid reports?
pairs.derivation: Megarian bulbs, the famous strengthening delicacy, from 'the Pelasgian city of Alcathous' — Alcathous' city = Megara, a standard poetic identification; food-trade realia verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ovaque sumantur, sumantur Hymettia mella, Quasque tulit folio pinus acuta nuces.
pairs.question: Cuius montis mella apud veteres laudatissima erant, ut apud Ovidium sumenda praecipiuntur?
pairs.question_en: Honey from which mountain was most prized among the ancients, as Ovid prescribes it be taken?
pairs.derivation: Hymettian honey, the proverbial best honey of antiquity (the Attic mountain), listed with eggs and pine nuts among wholesome fortifying foods. Verbatim epithet.

pairs.source_text: Nam modo Threicio Borea, modo currimus Euro, Saepe tument Zephyro lintea, saepe Noto.
pairs.question: Ex qua regione Boreas ventus flare putabatur, ut 'Threicius' a poetis diceretur?
pairs.question_en: From what region was the wind Boreas thought to blow, so that the poets call him 'Thracian'?
pairs.derivation: The north wind's canonical home in Thrace ('Threicio Borea'), part of the shared wind-lore (with Eurus, Zephyrus, Notus in the same couplet). Verbatim epithet; translatable geography.

pairs.source_text: Illa Machaonios superant medicamina sucos: His, ubi peccaris, restituendus eris.
pairs.question: Qua arte clarus erat Machaon, ut eius nomine suci medicati significentur?
pairs.question_en: For what art was Machaon famous, so that healing draughts are called by his name?
pairs.answer_en: For the art of healing (he was a physician).
pairs.derivation: Machaon, the healer of the Greeks at Troy (son of Asclepius), whose name stands for medicine itself ('Machaonios... sucos'). The usage presupposes the shared fact asked.

pairs.source_text: Duc, age, discipulos ad mea templa tuos, Est ubi diversum fama celebrata per orbem Littera, cognosci quae sibi quemque iubet.
pairs.question: Quid inscriptio illa, toto orbe celebrata, in templo Apollinis Delphici quemque facere iubet?
pairs.question_en: What does the world-famous inscription at Apollo's Delphic temple bid each person do?
pairs.derivation: The Delphic maxim 'know thyself' ('littera, cognosci quae sibi quemque iubet') at Apollo's temple — Apollo himself is the speaker ('mea templa'), and the Delphic setting is the canonical referent. Proverb of proverbs, verbatim in substance.

pairs.source_text: Haec tibi non hominem, sed quercus crede Pelasgas Dicere: nil istis ars mea maius habet.
pairs.question: Quae arbores apud Graecos oracula dare credebantur, quas 'Pelasgas quercus' Ovidius vocat?
pairs.question_en: Which trees among the Greeks were believed to give oracles, called 'Pelasgian oaks' by Ovid?
pairs.derivation: The speaking oaks of Dodona, the oldest Greek oracle — Ovid cites them as the voice of highest authority. 'Quercus Pelasgas dicere' verbatim; the Dodona identification is canonical.

pairs.source_text: Quot lepores in Atho, quot apes pascuntur in Hybla, Caerula quot bacas Palladis arbor habet,
pairs.question: Quo in monte Siculo apes plurimae pasci proverbio dicebantur?
pairs.question_en: On which Sicilian mountain were bees proverbially said to pasture in greatest numbers?
pairs.derivation: Hybla, the Sicilian mountain proverbial for its bees and honey, in Ovid's catalogue of countless things. Shared geography-lore; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quot lepores in Atho, quot apes pascuntur in Hybla, Caerula quot bacas Palladis arbor habet,
pairs.question: Quae arbor 'Palladis arbor' dicitur, quae bacas caerulas fert?
pairs.question_en: Which tree is called 'the tree of Pallas', bearing gray-green berries?
pairs.derivation: The olive as Minerva's/Pallas' tree ('caerula Palladis arbor'), her canonical gift and emblem. The periphrasis presupposes the shared fact asked; translatable.

pairs.source_text: Postibus et durae supplex blandire puellae, Et capiti demptas in fore pone rosas.
pairs.question: Quid amator exclusus in fore puellae ponere solebat?
pairs.question_en: What did the shut-out lover customarily leave on his girl's door?
pairs.answer_en: The roses (the garland) taken from his own head.
pairs.derivation: The paraklausithyron custom: the locked-out lover hangs his banquet garland on the doorpost. Courtship realia stated verbatim ('capiti demptas in fore pone rosas').

pairs.source_text: Fabula narratur toto notissima caelo, Mulciberis capti Marsque Venusque dolis.
pairs.question: Cuius dolis Mars et Venus capti sunt, ut notissima fabula narrat?
pairs.question_en: By whose wiles were Mars and Venus caught, as the very famous tale tells?
pairs.derivation: The Homeric tale (Od. 8) 'best known in all heaven': Vulcan trapping Mars and Venus in his invisible nets. All three names verbatim; Mulciber = Vulcan is the standard by-name.

pairs.source_text: Indicio Solis (quis Solem fallere possit?) Cognita Vulcano coniugis acta suae.
pairs.question: Cuius indicio Vulcanus adulterium Veneris coniugis cognovit?
pairs.question_en: By whose information did Vulcan learn of his wife Venus's adultery?
pairs.derivation: The Sun as the all-seeing informer of the Mars-Venus affair ('quis Solem fallere possit?') — canonical detail of the tale, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mulciber obscuros lectum circaque superque Disponit laqueos: lumina fallit opus. Fingit iter Lemnon; veniunt ad foedus amantes: Impliciti laqueis nudus uterque iacent.
pairs.question: Quo Vulcanus iter se facturum finxit, ut Martem et Venerem laqueis deciperet?
pairs.question_en: To where did Vulcan pretend he was journeying, in order to trap Mars and Venus in his snares?
pairs.derivation: The feigned trip to Lemnos, Vulcan's own island — canonical detail from Odyssey 8, verbatim ('fingit iter Lemnon').

pairs.source_text: Vix precibus, Neptune, tuis captiva resolvit Corpora: Mars Thracen occupat, illa Paphon.
pairs.question: Cuius dei precibus Vulcanus corpora Martis et Veneris captiva resolvit?
pairs.question_en: At which god's entreaties did Vulcan release the captive bodies of Mars and Venus?
pairs.derivation: Neptune's intercession freeing the trapped lovers — the Odyssey 8 detail kept by Ovid, verbatim ('precibus, Neptune, tuis').

pairs.source_text: Vix precibus, Neptune, tuis captiva resolvit Corpora: Mars Thracen occupat, illa Paphon.
pairs.question: Quas sedes Mars et Venus, laqueis Vulcani soluti, petiverunt?
pairs.question_en: To what seats did Mars and Venus withdraw when released from Vulcan's snares?
pairs.answer_en: Mars to Thrace, Venus to Paphos.
pairs.derivation: The canonical homes of the two gods — warlike Thrace for Mars, Paphos on Cyprus for Venus — stated verbatim as the tale's coda.

pairs.source_text: Quis Cereris ritus ausit vulgare profanis, Magnaque Threicia sacra reperta Samo?
pairs.question: Cuius deae ritus profanis vulgare nefas habebatur?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess's rites was it forbidden to divulge to the uninitiated?
pairs.derivation: The secrecy of the mysteries of Ceres (the Eleusinian rites) — cited by Ovid as the very type of what must be kept silent. Verbatim; cult-fact of shared religious knowledge.

pairs.source_text: Quis Cereris ritus ausit vulgare profanis, Magnaque Threicia sacra reperta Samo?
pairs.question: In qua insula, quam 'Threiciam Samon' Ovidius vocat, magna mysteria reperta sunt?
pairs.question_en: On which island, called 'Thracian Samos' by Ovid, were the great mysteries founded?
pairs.derivation: The mysteries of Samothrace ('Threicia Samos', the island's standard poetic name), ranked with Eleusis as inviolable rites. Verbatim periphrasis with a canonical referent.

pairs.source_text: O bene, quod frustra captatis arbore pomis Garrulus in media Tantalus aret aqua!
pairs.question: Qua poena Tantalus apud inferos adficitur?
pairs.answer: In media aqua sitit et poma frustra captat.
pairs.question_en: With what punishment is Tantalus afflicted in the underworld?
pairs.answer_en: He thirsts in the midst of water and snatches in vain at the fruit.
pairs.derivation: The canonical torment of Tantalus — water and fruit forever out of reach — which Ovid moralizes as the punishment of the 'garrulus' who betrayed divine secrets. Verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ipsa Venus pubem, quotiens velamina ponit, Protegitur laeva semireducta manu.
pairs.question: Qua manu Venus, velaminibus positis, se protegere fingitur?
pairs.question_en: With which hand is Venus, her garments laid aside, represented shielding herself?
pairs.derivation: The Venus Pudica pose of the famous statue type (the Cnidian and her Roman copies): the left hand half withdrawn to screen the body. Art-culture fact every Roman viewer knew; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec suus Andromedae color est obiectus ab illo, Mobilis in gemino cui pede pinna fuit.
pairs.question: Quis heros, cui pinna mobilis in gemino pede fuit, Andromedam uxorem habuit?
pairs.question_en: Which hero, who had a swift wing on each foot, had Andromeda as his wife?
pairs.derivation: Perseus identified by his canonical attribute, the winged sandals ('in gemino... pede pinna'), as Andromeda's husband who never reproached her dark color. Periphrasis with one referent.

pairs.source_text: Omnibus Andromache visa est spatiosior aequo: Unus, qui modicam diceret, Hector erat.
pairs.question: Qualis statura Andromache omnibus visa est, ut Ovidius refert?
pairs.question_en: Of what stature did Andromache seem to everyone, as Ovid relates?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's mythographic aside: Andromache seemed over-tall to all — only Hector called her 'modica'. Author-particular claim, hence attributed; verbatim and short.

pairs.source_text: Qui properant, nova musta bibant: mihi fundat avitum Consulibus priscis condita testa merum.
pairs.question: Quorum nominibus Romani vina condita notabant, ut vetustas constaret?
pairs.question_en: By whose names did the Romans mark their stored wines, so that the vintage's age was known?
pairs.derivation: Wine-jars dated by the consuls of the vintage year ('consulibus priscis condita testa') — the standard Roman vintage-dating custom, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Scilicet Hermionen Helenae praeponere posses, Et melior Gorge, quam sua mater, erat?
pairs.question: Cuius filia erat Hermione, quam matri praeponere nemo posset?
pairs.question_en: Whose daughter was Hermione, whom no one could rank above her mother?
pairs.derivation: Hermione as Helen's daughter — the point of Ovid's mother-daughter comparison. Canonical kinship fact; both names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quantus apud Danaos Podalirius arte medendi, Aeacides dextra, pectore Nestor erat,
pairs.question: Qua arte Podalirius inter Danaos excellebat?
pairs.question_en: In what art did Podalirius excel among the Greeks?
pairs.derivation: Podalirius (with his brother Machaon, son of Asclepius) the physician of the Greek host — 'arte medendi' verbatim in Ovid's catalogue of specialists.

pairs.source_text: Quantus erat Calchas extis, Telamonius armis, Automedon curru, tantus amator ego.
pairs.question: Qua arte Calchas apud Danaos praestabat?
pairs.question_en: In what art was Calchas preeminent among the Greeks?
pairs.answer_en: In reading entrails (he was the seer).
pairs.derivation: Calchas the diviner of the Greek host, 'great in entrails' ('Calchas extis'), beside Ajax ('Telamonius') in arms and Automedon with the chariot. Verbatim; short answer.

pairs.source_text: Arma dedi vobis: dederat Vulcanus Achilli; Vincite muneribus, vicit ut ille, datis.
pairs.question: Quis deus Achilli arma dederat?
pairs.question_en: Which god had given Achilles his arms?
pairs.derivation: Vulcan the maker of Achilles' divine armor (Iliad 18), the comparison Ovid draws for his own 'arms'. Both names verbatim; canonical fact.
